comments.value:
Maybe they could include a config file so we can decide what "Very Poor" actually is. No offense to the devs or Tupper, but when the system equates a user with a large bounds size to a user with several thousand avatars worth of active components, making them both "Very Poor", that system does me no good at all. I can't block "Very Poor" without seeing robots amongst all sorts of people, who just went a little over one or two limits. Often, that means their avatar isn't even intensive. For example, an avatar with 10,000 mesh particle poly is NOTHING. Even a Quest can handle that, since the particle meshes aren't even skinned mesh renderers, just normal meshes. That avatar wouldn't even need to have a body, or anything else, and would be called "Very Poor" merely for the poly count being over 5000 on a particle or multiple particles.

Meanwhile people who went insane, 20x over every limit, millions of poly on dozens of skinned meshes and particle systems with poly counts off the display, and hundreds of audio sources always active? Yeah, "Very Poor" as well. The system literally equates a performant Quest-capable avatar, with the most maliciously noncompliant ones you could design.

The whole avatar performance ranking system never made sense. It should've just been local benchmarking- the client knows how long it took to render each avatar, it can just show you the list of avatars and the time each cost so you can just hide the top ones. The benefit of this is that it takes into account everyone's particular hardware setup.

details:
While many veterans of the game tend to settle into friends+ worlds, I believe there is a significant portion of the community that enjoys -- or would like to enjoy -- the public world experience, and meeting new people.

I think the avatar ranking system was a huge step forward in this area. However, the sheer amount of variability in how avatars and models are built means that it can only go so far in determining users that are actually contributing significantly to performance drops. Two avatars with a Very Poor ranking can contribute a massively different amount of lag to a world, and while I understand the choice to factor hidden parts of an avatar into its performance rank, it undeniably blurs the line between what I'd consider an ethical creator of fun/interesting avatars, and one that doesn't know/care about the performance impact they're having on others.

In my experience, the major contributors to lag in a world usually comes down to one or two users. I've often found myself doing silent performance policing to determine who the "problem child" is, and it's almost always someone with avatar specs that run circles around the minimum threshhold of the Very Poor ranking, whether its due to 100+ meshes, 200+ materials, astronomical numbers of polys, etc. Doing this kind of avatar reconnaissance can be exhausting, and is an extremely manual process despite having access to all the necessary functions to do it. 

As much as I'd like to rely on the blanket performance rank blocking functions in place, this approach is actually more tedious, as the major contributors tend to be the minority, not the majority, of Very Poor ranked users, and forces an even bigger spam of "Show Avatar" on users that aren't contributing to lag significantly (some of which you may not want to have that set on universally). It results in the average user suffering more than the knowing/unknowing performance affecting user who would have their avatar blocked.

Since avatar performance ranking can never be an inherently perfect system for detecting the major performance contributors, I think it would be a lot more useful to be able to sort these users, ideally by the SEVERITY of their performance ranking statistics, rather than the performance ranking itself, though even the latter would be nice to have. 

There are a lot of things I'm not clear on as far as performance detection, as far as how on-demand or local the functionality for retrieving avatar stats is. Regardless, I've toyed around with ideas on how to make that sort query work efficiently. I can understand not wanting to add 50 more arbitrary performance ranks, but what about an internal "severity" ranking calculation for Very Poor avatars, since there's technically no limit to how "bad" an avatar can get performance-wise? Would it be too much overhead to calculate that on the fly, and if so, is it something that could be stored internally in the avatar stats? I don't know enough about the internal workings of the ranking system to know, but these are first steps in how I would personally approach the problem.

This feature request really just boils down to a way to filter out problematic users more effectively and to make public worlds a more survivable and consistent place to hang out, as that seems to have eroded somewhat over time even with the existing systems in place to mitigate these problems. I can understand how it's a slippery slope to account for every avatar that could cause performance issues, but I absolutely believe there is more progress to be made on this front, for the sake of the average user who simply wants to interact without encountering major performance issues on a consistent basis.
title: Sort Room Avatars by Performance Rank
